theory.overview: Assembly language is the bridge between high-level programming and raw machine code—the symbolic representation of instructions that processors execute directly. While programmers typically work in Python, Java, or C++, compilers translate those abstractions into assembly, then into binary that the CPU understands. Understanding assembly unlocks the black box of computation: you'll see how loops become conditional jumps, how functions use the stack, and how every variable access translates to memory operations. For embedded systems, performance optimization, security research, and reverse engineering, assembly remains an essential skill.

sections.title: From High Level to Machine Code
sections.content: The compilation process transforms human-readable code through multiple stages: source code → compiler → assembly → assembler → machine code → linker → executable. Assembly sits just above binary—each assembly instruction typically maps to one machine instruction. Unlike high-level languages with complex expressions and abstractions, assembly is explicit: every memory access, every arithmetic operation, every control transfer is visible and precisely specified.

sections.title: Instruction Categories
sections.content: Assembly instructions fall into categories: Data Movement (MOV, LOAD, STORE) transfer data between registers and memory; Arithmetic/Logic (ADD, SUB, AND, OR) perform computation; Control Flow (JMP, CALL, RET, conditional branches) alter execution sequence; Comparison/Testing (CMP, TEST) set flags for decisions; and System (SYSCALL, INT) interface with the operating system.

categories.arithmetic: ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, INC, DEC, NEG
categories.logic: AND, OR, XOR, NOT, SHL, SHR
categories.control: JMP, JE, JNE, CALL, RET, LOOP

sections.title: Registers: The Workspace
sections.content: Registers are the CPU's working memory—fast storage directly in the processor. x86-64 has 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers (RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, RBP, RSP, R8-R15), plus special-purpose registers like RIP (instruction pointer) and RFLAGS (status flags). RAX is the accumulator for arithmetic, RCX is the counter for loops, RSP is the stack pointer, RBP the base pointer for stack frames. Sub-registers access lower portions: EAX (32-bit), AX (16-bit), AH/AL (8-bit).

sections.title: Memory Addressing Modes
sections.content: Assembly provides flexible ways to access memory. Direct addressing uses a fixed address. Register indirect uses a register's value as address. Based addressing adds an offset to a base register. Indexed addressing uses an index register scaled by a multiplier (perfect for arrays). Combined modes offer [base + index*scale + offset], enabling efficient array and structure access.

sections.title: The Stack: Function Calls
sections.content: The stack is a LIFO memory region used for function calls, local variables, and saving state. RSP points to the top. PUSH decrements RSP and stores; POP loads and increments RSP. The CALL instruction pushes the return address and jumps to the function; RET pops and jumps back. The stack frame (bounded by RBP and RSP) holds local variables and saved registers. Understanding stack frames is crucial for debugging and security.

sections.title: System Calls and ABI
sections.content: The Application Binary Interface (ABI) defines how code interoperates: which registers hold arguments, which holds return values, how the stack is managed, and which registers must be preserved. For system calls, arguments go in specific registers (RDI, RSI, RDX, etc.), syscall number in RAX, then SYSCALL instruction traps to the kernel. Understanding the ABI is essential for interfacing assembly with C code or calling OS services.

keyConcepts.name: Mnemonic
keyConcepts.description: Human-readable name for an instruction. ADD, MOV, JMP are mnemonics.

keyConcepts.name: Opcode
keyConcepts.description: Binary code representing the operation. Machine-readable instruction.

keyConcepts.name: Operand
keyConcepts.description: Data operated on by an instruction. Can be register, memory, or immediate.

keyConcepts.name: Label
keyConcepts.description: Symbolic name for a memory address. Used for jumps, data, functions.

complexity.memoryAccess: O(1) to O(100+) depending on cache

steps.title: Understand Instruction Format
steps.description: Assembly: mnemonic destination, source. Example: MOV RAX, RBX copies RBX to RAX.

steps.title: Learn Addressing Modes
steps.description: Access memory via [base + index*scale + offset] for flexible data access.

steps.title: Master Stack Operations
steps.description: PUSH saves registers; POP restores. CALL/RET manage function entry/exit.

steps.title: Use System Calls
steps.description: Set arguments in registers per ABI, syscall number in RAX, execute SYSCALL.

practiceProblems.title: MOV Instruction
practiceProblems.description: What does MOV RAX, RBX do?
practiceProblems.answer: Copies value from RBX to RAX
practiceProblems.explanation: MOV copies data from source (RBX) to destination (RAX). The source is unchanged, destination gets a copy.

practiceProblems.title: PUSH Effect
practiceProblems.description: What happens to RSP when PUSH RAX executes?
practiceProblems.explanation: PUSH first decrements RSP by the operand size (8 for 64-bit), then stores the value at the new RSP address.

practiceProblems.title: CALL and RET
practiceProblems.description: What does CALL do before jumping to the function?
practiceProblems.explanation: CALL pushes the address of the next instruction (return address) onto the stack, then jumps to the function. RET pops this address to return.

practiceProblems.title: Memory Addressing
practiceProblems.description: If RAX=0x1000 and RBX=4, what address does [RAX + RBX*2 + 8] access?

practiceProblems.title: System Call ABI
practiceProblems.description: On Linux x86-64, which register holds the first argument for a system call?
practiceProblems.explanation: The System V AMD64 ABI specifies: RDI (1st arg), RSI (2nd), RDX (3rd), RCX (4th), R8 (5th), R9 (6th). RAX holds the syscall number.

practiceProblems.title: Loop in Assembly
practiceProblems.description: What does this code do? mov rcx, 5\nloop: dec rcx\njnz loop
practiceProblems.answer: Decrements RCX from 5 to 0 (loop runs 5 times)
practiceProblems.explanation: DEC decrements RCX. JNZ (jump if not zero) continues until RCX becomes 0. This is a simple countdown loop executing 5 times.

snippets.title: Hello World (Linux x86-64)
snippets.code:
; Hello World in x86-64 Assembly (Linux)
; Assemble: nasm -f elf64 hello.asm -o hello.o
; Link: ld hello.o -o hello

section .data
    msg db 'Hello, World!', 0x0A  ; String with newline
    len equ $ - msg              ; Calculate length

section .text
    global _start

_start:
    ; sys_write(stdout, msg, len)
    mov rax, 1          ; syscall: write
    mov rdi, 1          ; fd: stdout
    mov rsi, msg        ; buffer
    mov rdx, len        ; count
    syscall

    ; sys_exit(0)
    mov rax, 60         ; syscall: exit
    xor rdi, rdi        ; status: 0
    syscall

snippets.title: Function Example
snippets.code:
; Function that adds two numbers
; int64 add(int64 a, int64 b) -> a + b

section .text
global add

; Arguments: RDI = a, RSI = b
; Return: RAX = result
add:
    push rbp            ; Save old base pointer
    mov rbp, rsp        ; Set new base pointer
    
    mov rax, rdi        ; RAX = a
    add rax, rsi        ; RAX = a + b
    
    pop rbp             ; Restore base pointer
    ret                 ; Return (RAX has result)

; Caller code:
call_add:
    mov rdi, 10         ; First argument
    mov rsi, 20         ; Second argument
    call add            ; Call function
    ; Result in RAX = 30
